name: Government
description: A study of American government and political systems — the Constitution, three branches, civil liberties, political participation, public policy, and comparative government with global perspectives.

modules.title: Foundations of Government
modules.objectives: Explain the purposes of government; compare political philosophies of Locke, Hobbes, and Rousseau; identify major types of government.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §1.1 — purposes and forms of government
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Foundations of Government; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 1 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Use this supplied evidence set: Hobbes argues that insecurity in the state of nature makes strong authority necessary; Locke argues that people retain natural rights and may replace a government that violates them; Rousseau argues that legitimate law expresses the general will. Create a three-column comparison of human nature, purpose of government, and right to resist. Then write 250–350 words explaining which theory most clearly supports consent of the governed, citing at least two supplied statements. Submit: the comparison and analysis in one document or slide deck. Include: three accurate contrasts, two cited pieces of supplied evidence, and one limitation or counterargument. Evaluation: 100% total — accuracy 30%, use of evidence 30%, reasoning 25%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: The U.S. Constitution
modules.objectives: Describe the Constitutional Convention; explain the structure of the Constitution; analyze the amendment process and federalism. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §2.3 — Constitutional Convention, compromises, and structure
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — The U.S. Constitution; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 2 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Analyze this supplied convention case: State A has 900,000 residents, State B has 300,000, and both demand meaningful representation; delegates also dispute how enslaved people will be counted for representation and taxation, and whether Congress may regulate interstate and foreign commerce. Build a three-row chart for the Great, Three-Fifths, and Commerce compromises showing the dispute, the agreement, who gained power, and a long-term consequence. Finish with a 250-word judgment about which compromise most shaped the constitutional system. Submit: one chart plus the judgment. Include: all supplied disputes, historically accurate terms, and two course-reading citations. Evaluation: 100% total — accuracy 35%, consequence analysis 30%, evidence 20%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: The Bill of Rights & Civil Liberties
modules.objectives: Identify the freedoms protected by the First Amendment; explain due process and equal protection; analyze landmark Supreme Court civil liberties cases.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §4.1 — civil liberties and incorporation
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — The Bill of Rights & Civil Liberties; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 4 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Apply civil-liberties reasoning to this fictional school policy: a public school prohibits all shirts containing political messages after several peaceful students wear shirts supporting different causes; there is no evidence of disruption. Prepare a 350–450 word case brief identifying the relevant First Amendment principle, comparing the facts with Tinker v. Des Moines, presenting the school's strongest argument, and recommending a constitutional outcome. This is an academic exercise, not legal advice. Submit: a case brief with headings for Facts, Rule, Arguments, and Conclusion. Include: two facts that matter, the governing principle, both sides, and one cited course source. Evaluation: 100% total — rule accuracy 30%, application 35%, counterargument 20%, writing/citation 15%.

modules.title: The Legislative Branch
modules.objectives: Describe the bicameral structure of Congress; trace the lawmaking process; explain the role of committees and checks on Congress. Students will interpret sources or examples, explain cause-and-effect relationships, and support claims with evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §11.5 — how legislation moves through Congress
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — The Legislative Branch; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 11 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Trace this fictional bill: H.R. 410 is introduced in the House, referred to the Transportation Committee, amended and approved 24–18, passed the House 238–197, amended differently in the Senate, reconciled by a conference committee, approved again by both chambers, and sent to the president. Create a numbered flowchart showing every stage and identify three points where the bill could fail. Then explain in 200–250 words why committees and bicameral agreement matter. Submit: the flowchart and explanation. Include: all supplied stages, three failure points, and one check on Congress. Evaluation: 100% total — sequence 35%, institutional reasoning 30%, failure-point analysis 20%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: The Executive Branch
modules.objectives: Identify presidential powers enumerated in the Constitution; explain the role of the Cabinet and executive agencies; analyze the use and limits of executive orders.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §12.3 — executive organization, appointments, and governing
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — The Executive Branch; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 12 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Evaluate this fictional executive order: after a major storm, the president directs federal agencies to prioritize emergency bridge contracts using funds Congress already appropriated, but also attempts to create a new tax to finance future repairs. Write a 400-word analysis separating actions likely within executive authority from the action that requires Congress. Explain the constitutional or statutory limit, one possible judicial challenge, and one congressional response. Submit: a two-part authority table plus analysis. Include: each supplied action, at least two checks, and a reasoned conclusion. Evaluation: 100% total — power analysis 35%, checks and limits 30%, evidence 20%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: The Judicial Branch
modules.objectives: Describe the structure of the federal court system; explain judicial review; analyze landmark Supreme Court decisions and their impact.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §13.1 — federal courts and judicial review
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — The Judicial Branch; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 13 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Prepare a case brief from these supplied facts: William Marbury's commission was signed and sealed but not delivered; he asked the Supreme Court for a writ of mandamus under Section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789; Chief Justice Marshall concluded Marbury had a right and a remedy, but the Court lacked original jurisdiction because the statute conflicted with Article III. Submit: a 450-word case-brief report with Facts, Question, Holding, Reasoning, and Significance. Include: why Marbury did not receive the writ and how the decision established judicial review. Evaluation: 100% total — factual accuracy 30%, constitutional reasoning 35%, significance 20%, organization 15%.

modules.title: Federalism
modules.objectives: Distinguish enumerated, reserved, and concurrent powers; compare federal vs. state authority; explain the evolution of federalism from dual to cooperative to new federalism.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §3.1 — constitutional division of national and state powers
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Federalism; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 3 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Analyze this fictional federalism dispute: Congress requires national minimum cybersecurity safeguards for companies selling across state lines; State C adds stricter breach-notification rules for businesses operating inside the state. A company claims all state rules are preempted. Write a 400-word memo identifying the commerce, supremacy, and reserved-powers questions; explain when both rules might coexist and when conflict preemption might apply. Submit: a federal/state authority chart plus memo. Include: one argument for each government and a supported conclusion. Evaluation: 100% total — federalism concepts 35%, application 35%, counterarguments 15%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Political Parties & Elections
modules.objectives: Explain how political parties organize presidential nominations; distinguish primaries, caucuses, conventions, and the general election; trace how the Electoral College formally selects the president.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §12.2 — primaries, caucuses, conventions, the general election, and the Electoral College
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Political Parties & Elections; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 12 review questions — focus on the presidential nomination and election-process items
modules.assignment: Create a four-stage process map showing primaries/caucuses, national conventions, the general election, and the Electoral College. Then analyze this fictional result: Candidate Cedar wins regions worth 110, 95, and 70 electoral votes and receives 48.9 million popular votes; Candidate Harbor wins regions worth 135 and 128 electoral votes and receives 50.1 million popular votes. Identify the electoral winner and explain why the national popular-vote leader need not win. Submit: the process map, calculations, and 300-word explanation. Include: the role of parties and delegates, the 270-vote threshold, and one advantage or criticism of the Electoral College. Evaluation: 100% total — process accuracy 30%, calculation 25%, institutional reasoning 30%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Voting, Campaigns & Political Participation
modules.objectives: Analyze factors affecting voter turnout; explain campaign finance rules; assess the impact of gerrymandering and identify ways citizens engage in civic life.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §7.1 — registration and participation barriers
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Voting, Campaigns & Political Participation; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 7 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Analyze this fictional turnout table: ages 18–29, 44%; 30–49, 58%; 50–64, 68%; 65+, 72%. Registration is 12 percentage points lower in the youngest group, while reported interest in local issues differs by only 3 points. Write a 350-word evidence memo identifying two plausible mechanisms, one claim the data cannot prove, and one nonpartisan intervention that targets registration rather than a political group. Submit: one chart and the memo. Include: at least three numerical comparisons and a causation warning. Evaluation: 100% total — data accuracy 30%, inference quality 30%, intervention design 25%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Public Policy Process
modules.objectives: Trace the stages of the policy process — agenda setting, formation, adoption, implementation, and evaluation; apply the model to a real policy example.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §16.1 — public policy and the policy process
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Public Policy Process; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 16 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Apply the policy cycle to this supplied case: a city reports missed medical appointments because two neighborhoods lack evening transit; advocates place the issue on the agenda; council staff design a voucher pilot; the council funds a six-month trial; the transit agency implements it; evaluators compare appointment completion before and after. Create a five-stage policy-cycle table and propose two outcome measures plus one fairness measure. Submit: the table and a 250-word evaluation plan. Include: actors, decision points, measures, and one implementation risk. Evaluation: 100% total — stage accuracy 30%, measures 30%, implementation analysis 25%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Civil Rights Movements & the Law
modules.objectives: Explain the role of the 14th Amendment in extending rights; analyze landmark civil rights legislation; evaluate the ongoing struggles for equality.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §5.1 — identifying civil-rights claims and unequal treatment
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Civil Rights Movements & the Law; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 5 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Compare three supplied civil-rights strategies: litigation challenging unequal law, nonviolent protest that raises public attention, and legislation that creates enforceable national rules. Using Brown v. Board of Education, the Birmingham campaign, and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 as course examples, write a 500-word analysis of how the strategies reinforced one another. Submit: a strategy-evidence-outcome table plus the analysis. Include: one strength and limitation of each strategy and two cited course sources. Evaluation: 100% total — historical accuracy 30%, comparative reasoning 35%, evidence 20%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Foreign Policy & National Security
modules.objectives: Identify the tools of U.S. foreign policy; explain the roles of NATO, the UN, and the military; analyze how diplomacy, sanctions, and aid are used to advance national interests.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §17.2 — diplomatic, economic, and military instruments
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Foreign Policy & National Security; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 17 review questions — complete the items connected to this module before the quiz
modules.assignment: Advise leaders in this fictional crisis: Country R blocks humanitarian deliveries to a neighboring state; the United States seeks access without escalating armed conflict. Options are diplomatic negotiations, targeted financial sanctions, humanitarian aid through international organizations, and military force. Build a decision matrix rating legality/authority, likely effectiveness, civilian risk, reversibility, and need for congressional action. Recommend a sequenced response in 400 words. Submit: the matrix and recommendation. Include: evidence from the supplied facts, all four tools, executive and congressional roles, and one uncertainty. Evaluation: 100% total — tool accuracy 30%, trade-off analysis 35%, branch-role analysis 20%, clarity 15%.

modules.title: Economic Policy & the Budget
modules.objectives: Define fiscal policy; explain how the federal budget is created; distinguish mandatory from discretionary spending; analyze the causes and consequences of the national debt.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax American Government 3e §16.5 — federal budgeting, mandatory and discretionary spending, fiscal policy, taxes, and monetary policy
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Economic Policy & the Budget; use with the assigned reading and module evidence task
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Chapter 16 review questions — focus on deficit, debt, mandatory spending, and fiscal-policy items before the quiz
modules.assignment: Use this fictional federal budget (billions): revenue—individual income tax 2,400, payroll tax 1,600, corporate tax 500, other 300; spending—Social Security 1,500, health programs 1,700, defense 900, safety-net programs 500, interest 700, other discretionary 800. Calculate total revenue, total spending, and the deficit or surplus. Propose one change worth 200–400 billion and explain who benefits, who bears the cost, and one objection. Submit: calculations, a labeled chart, and a 350-word policy note. Include: mandatory/discretionary classification for four items and transparent assumptions. Evaluation: 100% total — calculations 30%, classification 20%, trade-off reasoning 35%, clarity 15%.

questions.question: Which philosopher argued that people enter a social contract to escape the brutish 'state of nature'?
questions.answer: Thomas Hobbes
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Thomas Hobbes. It connects the correct answer to Government midterm concepts and separates it from plausible distractors.

questions.question: The principle of popular sovereignty means that:
options: Government power derives from the consent of the governed
Congress can override any court decision
States have power over the federal government
questions.answer: Government power derives from the consent of the governed
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Government power derives from the consent of the governed.

questions.question: The Great Compromise at the Constitutional Convention created:
options: A bicameral legislature with proportional House seats and equal Senate seats
questions.answer: A bicameral legislature with proportional House seats and equal Senate seats
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: A bicameral legislature with proportional House seats and equal Senate seats.

questions.question: Why was the Bill of Rights added to the Constitution?
options: To protect individual freedoms from government overreach
To create the office of president
To give Congress unlimited power to tax
To replace the Articles of Confederation with a monarchy
questions.answer: To protect individual freedoms from government overreach
questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights lists protections for individual liberties and limits certain government actions.

questions.question: Which First Amendment freedom protects citizens' right to criticize the government?
options: Freedom of the press and speech
questions.answer: Freedom of the press and speech
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Freedom of the press and speech. Students need to recognize why Freedom of the press and speech matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

questions.question: A bill introduced in the House of Representatives must pass through which body before becoming law?
questions.answer: The Senate
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: The Senate. It ties the answer to the historical, civic, geographic, or economic concept being assessed.

questions.question: Which pair consists of powers primarily reserved to state governments under the Tenth Amendment?
options: Establishing local governments and issuing professional licenses
Negotiating treaties and regulating foreign commerce
Naturalizing citizens and maintaining armed forces
questions.answer: Establishing local governments and issuing professional licenses
questions.explanation: The Constitution delegates the other listed powers to the national government; local-government structure and professional licensing generally remain state responsibilities.

questions.question: Presidential veto power is an example of:
questions.answer: Checks and balances
questions.explanation: A veto lets the president check Congress, while Congress may override a veto with enough votes.

questions.question: The Cabinet members are appointed by the president and must be confirmed by:
questions.answer: The Senate
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: The Senate. Students need to recognize why The Senate matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

questions.question: Judicial review — the power to strike down unconstitutional laws — was established by:
questions.answer: Marbury v. Madison (1803)
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Marbury v. Madison (1803). This reinforces the Government midterm concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: Enumerated powers are powers:
options: Shared between federal and state governments
Specifically listed in the Constitution as belonging to Congress
questions.answer: Specifically listed in the Constitution as belonging to Congress
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Specifically listed in the Constitution as belonging to Congress.

questions.question: The Supremacy Clause states that:
options: State constitutions always override federal law
Federal law is the supreme law of the land when made under the Constitution
The president can suspend the Constitution during elections
The Supreme Court writes all federal statutes
questions.answer: Federal law is the supreme law of the land when made under the Constitution
questions.explanation: The Supremacy Clause makes the Constitution and valid federal laws supreme over conflicting state laws.

questions.question: Explain the concept of 'separation of powers' and provide one example of how each branch checks another branch of government.
questions.answer: Separation of powers assigns legislative, executive, and judicial authority to different branches. Examples include the president vetoing a bill (executive checks legislative), Congress overriding a veto or confirming nominees (legislative checks executive), and courts invalidating unconstitutional laws or executive actions (judicial checks the elected branches).
questions.explanation: A complete answer must identify the three branches and correctly label at least one check exercised by each branch; examples should not reverse which branch is doing the checking.

questions.question: The due process clause of the 14th Amendment has been used to:
options: Apply most Bill of Rights protections to state governments
Grant Congress power to regulate interstate commerce
questions.answer: Apply most Bill of Rights protections to state governments
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Apply most Bill of Rights protections to state governments.

questions.question: Describe the process by which the Constitution can be amended. Why did the Founders make this process difficult?
questions.answer: An amendment requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress (or a constitutional convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures), then ratification by three-fourths (38) of state legislatures or state conventions. The Founders made it difficult to protect fundamental rights from temporary majorities, ensure broad national consensus, and maintain constitutional stability.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: An amendment requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress (or a constitutional convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures), then ratification by three-fourths (38) of state legislatures or state conventions. The Founders made it difficult to protect fundamental rights from temporary majorities, ensure broad national consensus, and maintain constitutional stability..

questions.question: John Locke's idea that government should protect life, liberty, and property most directly influenced:
options: The Declaration of Independence's natural-rights language
The Federalist Papers' defense of a strong executive only
The creation of the modern income tax
The Twenty-Sixth Amendment lowering the voting age
questions.answer: The Declaration of Independence's natural-rights language
questions.explanation: Locke's natural-rights theory strongly influenced the Declaration of Independence's language about rights and legitimate government.

questions.question: The Federalist Papers were written to:
options: Argue for a Bill of Rights only
Persuade New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution
questions.answer: Persuade New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Persuade New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution. Students need to recognize why Persuade New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

questions.question: The exclusionary rule (established in Mapp v. Ohio) states that:
options: Evidence obtained illegally cannot be used in court
Suspects must be informed of their rights before questioning
Citizens cannot be tried twice for the same crime
The government must provide lawyers for those who cannot afford one
questions.answer: Evidence obtained illegally cannot be used in court
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Evidence obtained illegally cannot be used in court.

questions.question: A filibuster in the U.S. Senate is a tactic used to:
options: Delay or block legislation through extended debate
questions.answer: Delay or block legislation through extended debate
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Delay or block legislation through extended debate. Students need to recognize why Delay or block legislation through extended debate matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

questions.question: Executive orders are issued by the president and generally:
options: Direct executive branch action while remaining subject to constitutional and statutory limits
Can amend the Constitution without approval
Automatically override all Supreme Court decisions
Are written and passed by Congress before the president signs them
questions.answer: Direct executive branch action while remaining subject to constitutional and statutory limits
questions.explanation: Executive orders guide executive branch operations but must stay within constitutional and legal authority and may be challenged in court.

questions.question: The Supreme Court's decision in Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned:
options: Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine
questions.answer: Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Plessy v. Ferguson's 'separate but equal' doctrine. The explanation asks students to connect the answer with cause, evidence, or consequence rather than memorizing a term.

questions.question: An unfunded mandate occurs when:
options: The federal government raises taxes without Congressional approval
Congress requires states to implement a program without providing funds
A state refuses to follow a Supreme Court ruling
The president signs a bill into law without reading it
questions.answer: Congress requires states to implement a program without providing funds
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Congress requires states to implement a program without providing funds.

questions.question: In a primary election, voters typically:
options: Choose between the Democratic and Republican nominees
Select their party's candidate for the general election
questions.answer: Select their party's candidate for the general election
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Select their party's candidate for the general election.

questions.question: In Government final concepts, Gerrymandering refers to:
options: Drawing electoral district boundaries to favor a party or group
Requiring citizens to register before voting
Counting electoral votes after a presidential election
Holding a primary election before a general election
questions.answer: Drawing electoral district boundaries to favor a party or group
questions.explanation: Gerrymandering is the manipulation of district boundaries for political advantage.

questions.question: Agenda setting in the public policy process refers to:
options: Determining which issues government will address
Evaluating whether a policy achieved its goals
questions.answer: Determining which issues government will address
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Determining which issues government will address. This reinforces the Government final concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibited discrimination based on:
options: Race, color, religion, sex, and national origin
questions.answer: Race, color, religion, sex, and national origin
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Race, color, religion, sex, and national origin. It ties the answer to the historical, civic, geographic, or economic concept being assessed.

questions.question: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is primarily:
options: A collective-defense alliance among member states in Europe and North America
A global economic trading bloc administered by the United Nations
A United Nations peacekeeping force with universal membership
An agreement requiring members to share nuclear-weapons technology
questions.answer: A collective-defense alliance among member states in Europe and North America
questions.explanation: NATO is a regional collective-defense alliance; Article 5 treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all, while each member determines the action it deems necessary.

questions.question: Mandatory spending in the federal budget includes programs such as:
options: Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid entitlements
Only foreign aid grants approved each year
Only salaries for members of Congress
questions.answer: Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid entitlements
questions.explanation: Mandatory spending is required by existing law and includes major entitlement programs such as Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.

questions.question: In a parliamentary system, the head of government (prime minister) is:
options: Elected directly by voters in a national election
Appointed by the head of state without legislative input
The leader of the majority party or coalition in the legislature
questions.answer: The leader of the majority party or coalition in the legislature
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: The leader of the majority party or coalition in the legislature.

questions.question: The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) allows citizens to:
options: Sue the president without congressional approval
questions.answer: Request access to government records
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Request access to government records. It connects the correct answer to Government final concepts and separates it from plausible distractors.

questions.question: Fiscal policy refers to government use of:
options: Taxation and spending to influence the economy
questions.answer: Taxation and spending to influence the economy
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Taxation and spending to influence the economy. It connects the correct answer to Government final concepts and separates it from plausible distractors.

questions.question: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was designed to:
options: Eliminate discriminatory practices that blocked Black Americans from voting
Require every state to use the same ballot design
questions.answer: Eliminate discriminatory practices that blocked Black Americans from voting
questions.explanation: The Voting Rights Act targeted discriminatory barriers such as literacy tests and other practices used to suppress Black voting rights.

questions.question: Compare the U.S. presidential system with a parliamentary system on two dimensions: how the executive is chosen and how the executive can be removed from office.
questions.answer: In the U.S. presidential system, the president is elected separately by voters (via the Electoral College) for a fixed four-year term and can only be removed through the impeachment process (House impeaches, Senate convicts with two-thirds vote). In a parliamentary system, the prime minister is chosen by the legislature — typically the leader of the majority party — and can be removed through a vote of no confidence at any time, allowing more flexible and responsive governance.
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: In the U.S. presidential system, the president is elected separately by voters (via the Electoral College) for a fixed four-year term and can only be removed through the impeachment process (House impeaches, Senate convicts with two-thirds vote). In a parliamentary system, the prime minister is chosen by the legislature — typically the leader of the majority party — and can be removed through a vote of no confidence at any time, allowing more flexible and responsive governance..

questions.question: A democracy index typically measures countries on criteria including:
options: GDP per capita and military strength
Electoral process, civil liberties, government functioning, and political participation
Trade surplus and foreign aid given
Number of political parties and voter registration rates alone
questions.answer: Electoral process, civil liberties, government functioning, and political participation
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Electoral process, civil liberties, government functioning, and political participation.

questions.question: Explain how campaign finance laws (e.g., Citizens United v. FEC) affect political participation and democratic equality.
questions.answer: Citizens United v. FEC held that government may not prohibit independent political expenditures by corporations and unions; it did not authorize direct corporate contributions to candidates. Supporters argue independent spending is protected political speech. Critics argue unequal resources can create unequal influence and reduce perceived democratic equality. A strong answer distinguishes independent expenditures from direct contributions and evaluates both perspectives.
questions.explanation: Credit requires the independent-expenditure/direct-contribution distinction plus a supported discussion of participation or equality; treating all corporate contributions as unlimited is inaccurate.

quizQuestions.question: According to John Locke, the primary purpose of government is to:
options: Protect natural rights of life, liberty, and property
quizQuestions.answer: Protect natural rights of life, liberty, and property
quizQuestions.explanation: The correct answer is: Protect natural rights of life, liberty, and property.

quizQuestions.question: Thomas Hobbes described life without government as:
options: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short
quizQuestions.answer: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short
quizQuestions.explanation: The correct answer is: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. It connects the correct answer to Foundations of Government and separates it from plausible distractors.

quizQuestions.question: John Locke's political theory most directly influenced which idea in the Declaration of Independence?
options: Governments derive just powers from the consent of the governed
The president should serve a lifetime term
quizQuestions.answer: Governments derive just powers from the consent of the governed
quizQuestions.explanation: Locke's ideas about natural rights and consent influenced the Declaration's claim that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Which type of government is defined by rule by a small, elite group?
quizQuestions.answer: Oligarchy
quizQuestions.explanation: A correct response identifies "Oligarchy" and connects it to the module context.

quizQuestions.question: The Constitutional Convention was held in:
quizQuestions.answer: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania
quizQuestions.explanation: The correct answer is: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. The explanation asks students to connect the answer with cause, evidence, or consequence rather than memorizing a term.

quizQuestions.question: The Preamble to the Constitution begins with the words:
options: 'We the People of the United States…'
'When in the course of human events…'
quizQuestions.answer: 'We the People of the United States…'
quizQuestions.explanation: The correct answer is: 'We the People of the United States…'. It ties the answer to the historical, civic, geographic, or economic concept being assessed.

quizQuestions.question: The Three-Fifths Compromise counted enslaved people as:
options: Three-fifths of a person for representation and taxation
Equal to free citizens only for taxation
quizQuestions.answer: Three-fifths of a person for representation and taxation
quizQuestions.explanation: The correct answer is: Three-fifths of a person for representation and taxation.

quizQuestions.question: The Constitution’s Supremacy Clause establishes that:
options: Valid federal law prevails when it conflicts with state law
State constitutions always override federal statutes
The president may suspend any court ruling
Only local governments may regulate elections
quizQuestions.answer: Valid federal law prevails when it conflicts with state law
quizQuestions.explanation: Article VI makes the Constitution, valid federal laws, and treaties the supreme law of the land, so conflicting state law must yield.

quizQuestions.question: The First Amendment protects all of the following EXCEPT:
quizQuestions.answer: Freedom from unreasonable searches
quizQuestions.explanation: The correct answer is: Freedom from unreasonable searches. Students need to recognize why Freedom from unreasonable searches matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

quizQuestions.question: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled that:
options: Students retain First Amendment rights unless expression materially disrupts school or invades others’ rights
Schools may ban every political message without evidence of disruption
Only college students have constitutional speech rights
Student speech is protected only outside school grounds
quizQuestions.answer: Students retain First Amendment rights unless expression materially disrupts school or invades others’ rights
quizQuestions.explanation: Tinker protects student expression while allowing schools to regulate speech that causes a material and substantial disruption or infringes others’ rights.

quizQuestions.question: The Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination means:
options: You cannot be arrested without a warrant
You cannot be forced to testify against yourself
You have the right to an attorney
